+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 28.4
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan sat in the plush, cushioned seat of the transfer vessel, his reflection staring back at him from the polished metal surface of the bulkhead. The hum of the air filtration system was a constant reminder of the vessel's artificial environment, a stark contrast to the dusty, rugged landscape of Mars he had known all his life. The seat was too comfortable, the air too clean, and the silence too oppressive. It was all a far cry from the clanking, grinding machinery of the mining operations he was used to. The vessel was sleek and modern, a testament to the technological advancements that had made interstellar travel possible. The walls were adorned with holographic displays, flickering with data streams and navigation charts. The insignia of the Antares diplomatic corps was emblazoned on the bulkhead, a stylized starburst that seemed to mock the very idea of diplomacy. Arthur had seen enough of the corps' operations to know that their methods were anything but diplomatic. As the vessel glided through the void, Arthur's mind raced with questions. Who was this unknown party that had summoned him? What did they want with him and the Azra vein he had discovered? And why the sudden interest from the Antares corps, an organization known more for its covert operations than its diplomatic efforts? The transfer vessel docked with a gentle thud, and the airlock hissed open, revealing a corridor bathed in soft, blue light. Arthur stepped out, his boots sinking slightly into the plush carpeting. He was greeted by a tall, imposing figure in a crisp, black uniform, the insignia of the Antares corps gleaming on his chest. "Mr. Neegan," the figure said, his voice deep and authoritative. "I am Commander Voss. Welcome aboard the *Diplomat's Wrath*. Please follow me." Arthur followed Commander Voss through the labyrinthine corridors of the vessel, the hum of machinery and the distant murmur of voices echoing around them. They passed through a series of security checkpoints, each one more elaborate than the last. Arthur couldn't help but feel like a prisoner, despite the polite demeanor of his escorts. Finally, they arrived at a large, ornate chamber. The walls were adorned with holographic displays, showing real-time data streams and strategic maps. In the center of the room was a large, circular table, around which several figures were seated. They turned to face Arthur as he entered, their expressions a mix of curiosity and calculation. "Mr. Neegan," one of the figures said, rising from his seat. He was an older man, his hair silver and his eyes sharp. "I am Ambassador Kael. Welcome to the *Diplomat's Wrath*. Please, have a seat." Arthur took a seat at the table, his heart pounding in his chest. He felt like a pawn in a game he didn't understand, a game where the stakes were higher than he could imagine. "Mr. Neegan," Ambassador Kael began, his voice smooth and measured. "We have called you here today because of your recent discovery on Mars. The Azra vein you have uncovered is of great strategic importance, and we believe it could play a crucial role in the future of interstellar travel and defense." Arthur nodded, his mind racing. "I see. And what exactly do you want from me?" Ambassador Kael leaned forward, his eyes locked on Arthur's. "We want you to work with us, Mr. Neegan. We want you to help us unlock the secrets of Azra, to harness its power for the benefit of all." Arthur raised an eyebrow. "All? Or just the Antares corps?" Ambassador Kael's expression didn't change. "The Antares corps is but one part of a larger alliance, Mr. Neegan. An alliance dedicated to the preservation of peace and stability in the galaxy. But we cannot do this alone. We need your expertise, your knowledge of Azra. We need you to help us build a better future." Arthur leaned back in his seat, his mind whirling. He had always been a miner, a man of the dirt and the machines. He had never imagined himself as a pawn in a game of galactic politics. But here he was, sitting in a room full of diplomats and soldiers, being asked to help shape the future of the galaxy. "But why me?" Arthur asked, his voice steady despite the turmoil inside him. "There are other engineers, other experts. Why do you need me?" Ambassador Kael smiled, a cold, calculating smile. "Because, Mr. Neegan, you are the one who discovered the Azra vein. You are the one who understands it, who knows its secrets. And because we believe that you, of all people, have the potential to be a leader in this new era." Arthur felt a shiver run down his spine. He had always been a man of action, a doer. He had never been one for politics or diplomacy. But here he was, being asked to take on a role he had never imagined for himself. "And what if I refuse?" Arthur asked, his voice steady. "What if I don't want to be a part of your alliance?" Ambassador Kael's smile faded, and his eyes hardened. "Then, Mr. Neegan, I'm afraid we will have no choice but to take more... drastic measures. The Azra vein is too important to be left in the hands of a single individual. It must be controlled, harnessed, and used for the greater good." Arthur felt a cold chill run down his spine. He had always known that the discovery of Azra would change his life, but he had never imagined it would lead him to this point. He was caught in a web of politics and intrigue, a web that he had no idea how to escape. "But what about the other corporations?" Arthur asked, his mind racing. "What about the other interests vying for control of Azra? What about the arms race?" Ambassador Kael's expression didn't change. "The other corporations are but pawns in a larger game, Mr. Neegan. They are tools to be used, and discarded when they are no longer needed. The arms race is a necessary evil, a means to an end. But in the end, it is the alliance that will prevail, and it is the alliance that will shape the future of the galaxy." Arthur felt a sense of dread wash over him. This is a clear generation loop, destroying coherence and pacing. The dialogue is flat and expository — Ambassador Kael speaks in generic villain platitudes ("necessary evil," "greater good," "part of history") with no subtext, wit, or Asimovian intellectual sparring. Asimov's style is characterized by idea-driven dialogue, logical deduction, and understated big-picture sociopolitical reasoning; none of that is present. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 51.6
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom was our sanctuary, a cramped space filled with the hum of the ventilation fan and the faint, acrid scent of developer. The red safelight cast everything in a warm, eerie glow, like we were suspended in some limbo between day and night. Elliot and I had been paired for our final project, a series of photographs exploring the theme of "Self-Discovery." Ironically, it was Elliot who was doing most of the discovering—and I was right there with him, trying to make sense of it all. Elliot was bent over the enlarger, his thrift-store band t-shirt draped over his lean frame, sleeves rolled up to reveal tattoos that snaked up his forearms. His fingers, long and delicate, adjusted the lens with a precision that belied his soft demeanor. I watched him, my heart pounding in a way that was both exhilarating and terrifying. "I've been thinking about something," Elliot said, his voice barely above a whisper. He kept his eyes on the enlarger, but I could see the tension in his shoulders. I leaned against the counter, trying to keep my voice steady. "Yeah? What's that?" He took a deep breath. "About who I am. Who I want to be." I felt a surge of protectiveness. Elliot was so gentle, so fragile in his own way. I wanted to shield him from the world, to make sure no one ever hurt him. But I also knew I needed to give him space, to let him find his own path. "What do you mean?" I asked, trying to keep my tone neutral. Elliot finally looked up at me, his eyes reflecting the red light. "I think I might be non-binary," he said, the words tumbling out in a rush. "Or maybe genderfluid. I don't know. I'm still figuring it out." I felt a mixture of excitement and confusion. Elliot's journey was fascinating, but it also challenged everything I thought I knew about myself. I'd always been drawn to traditional masculinity, to the strong, assertive men who took charge in the bedroom and out. But Elliot... Elliot was different. He was soft and vulnerable, and yet there was a strength in him that I couldn't ignore. "I think it's amazing that you're exploring this," I said, meaning every word. "It takes a lot of courage to question yourself like that." Elliot smiled, a small, tentative curve of his lips. "Thanks. It's just... it's hard, you know? I don't want people to see me differently." I stepped closer, my voice dropping to a hush. "You don't have to tell anyone until you're ready. This is your journey, Elliot. No one else's." He nodded, his eyes never leaving mine. The air between us was charged, electric. I could feel the pull, the undeniable chemistry that had been building for weeks. "And what about you?" Elliot asked, his voice barely a whisper. I hesitated, caught off guard. "What about me?" "Have you ever questioned... anything?" he asked, his eyes searching mine. I shook my head, a nervous laugh escaping my lips. "No. I mean, I've always known who I am. Or at least, I thought I did." Elliot reached out, his fingers brushing against mine. The touch was feather-light, but it sent a shockwave through my body. "Maybe it's not about knowing," he said softly. "Maybe it's about discovering." I swallowed hard, my heart pounding in my chest. "Maybe," I whispered. The moment was broken by the accidental exposure of a stack of photo paper. The paper, left out in the red light for too long, was now ruined, the surface marred by light leaks. I cursed under my breath, my usual assertiveness returning as I scrambled to salvage what I could. "Shit, that's a waste of paper," I muttered, tossing the ruined sheets into the trash. Elliot laughed, a soft, melodic sound that filled the darkroom. "It's okay," he said. "We'll just have to make more." I looked at him, his eyes shining in the red light, and felt a surge of affection. He was right. We would make more. We would keep exploring, keep discovering, together. As we cleaned up the darkroom, the tension between us was palpable. I wanted to reach out, to touch him, to explore this newfound connection. But I held back, giving Elliot the space he needed. "Dani," he said, his voice soft but firm. "Can I ask you something?" I turned to him, my heart in my throat. "Of course." "Would you... would you want to go out with me?" he asked, his eyes never leaving mine. "Like, on a date?" I felt a rush of excitement and fear. This was uncharted territory for me, but the thought of exploring it with Elliot was exhilarating. "Yes," I said, my voice steady despite the turmoil inside me. "I'd like that." Elliot's face broke into a wide grin, and I couldn't help but smile back. The red light cast a warm glow over us, sealing our moment in this intimate, confessional space. As we left the darkroom, the world outside seemed brighter, more vibrant. I felt a sense of possibility, of adventure. Elliot and I were stepping into the unknown, but we were doing it together. And as we walked side by side, our shoulders brushing, I knew that whatever happened, whatever we discovered, it would be worth it. Because this was more than just a project, more than just a crush. This was a journey of self-discovery, and I was glad to be on it with Elliot. The next few weeks were a whirlwind of dates and darkroom sessions. Elliot and I explored the city, finding hidden gems and secret spots that seemed to exist just for us. We talked for hours, sharing our dreams, our fears, our hopes. And in the darkroom, we created art that reflected our journey, our connection. But as the semester drew to a close, I found myself wrestling with my own identity. I'd always been so sure of who I was, of what I wanted. But Elliot had challenged that, had shown me that there was more to life than the labels and expectations I'd grown up with. One night, as we sat in the darkroom, the enlarger humming softly, I turned to Elliot. "I've been thinking," I said, my voice hesitant. He looked at me, his eyes reflecting the red light. "About what?" "About us," I said. "About me. About who I am." Elliot reached out, his hand covering mine. "You don't have to figure it out all at once," he said softly. "It's okay to take your time." I nodded, feeling a sense of relief. "I know. It's just... it's hard. I've always been so sure of myself, and now... now I'm not so sure." Elliot smiled, his thumb tracing circles on the back of my hand. "That's okay, Dani. It's okay to be unsure. It's okay to explore. It's okay to be... us." I felt a surge of love for him, for his gentleness, his understanding. He was giving me the space to figure it out, to discover who I was without judgment or pressure. "And what about you?" I asked, my voice soft. "Are you sure about... everything?" Elliot nodded, his eyes never leaving mine. "I'm sure that I want to be me," he said. "And I'm sure that I want to be with you." I felt a rush of emotion, a mixture of love and fear and excitement. This was uncharted territory, but I was ready to explore it. With Elliot by my side, I knew I could face anything. As we finished our final prints, the darkroom filled with the soft glow of the enlarger, I felt a sense of accomplishment. We had created something beautiful, something that reflected our journey, our connection. And as we left the darkroom, hand in hand, I knew that this was just the beginning. Our journey of self-discovery was far from over, but I was excited to see where it would take us. Together, Elliot and I would explore the unknown, challenge our assumptions, and create a future that was uniquely ours. And in the end, wasn't that what life was all about? Discovering who we are, one step at a time.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the basic prompt requirements: first-person Dani, darkroom setting, Elliot's gender questioning, Dani's internal conflict between assertiveness and protectiveness. However, execution is uneven. The prose leans heavily on telling ("I felt a surge of protectiveness," "I felt a mixture of excitement and confusion") rather than dramatizing emotion through action or sensory detail. The darkroom setting is a strong choice but underused—the photography process is mostly backdrop, with the ruined photo paper serving as a convenient, somewhat clumsy tension-breaker. The dialogue is serviceable but generic. Lines like "Maybe it's not about knowing... Maybe it's about discovering" and "It's okay to be... us" feel like therapy-speak rather than how two art students would actually talk. Elliot's confession arrives almost immediately and without real tentativeness, undercutting the "tender awkwardness" the prompt requested. The chemistry is asserted rather than built. Structurally, the story meanders badly in its second half. After the date acceptance—a natural ending point—it continues through weeks of dating, another identity crisis for Dani, and a second near-identical ending. This repetition dilutes the emotional payoff. The final paragraphs pile on tidy affirmations ("wasn't that what life was all about?") that feel unearned and saccharine. Dani's identity confusion is stated repeatedly but never explored with specificity—what does it actually feel like to be attracted to someone whose gender presentation is shifting? The story gestures at this but resolves it with vague reassurance. Elliot remains a soft, gentle cipher; his nu-goth style and intellect are mentioned but never demonstrated. The prose itself is clean and readable, with occasional nice touches (the safelight's "limbo between day and night"), but also clichés ("heart pounding," "eyes reflecting the red light" appears twice, "uncharted territory" twice). The ending positivity is incongruent with the genuine uncertainty the story claims to explore—everything is resolved with a bow. Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
In the heart of Rome, where ancient cobblestones met the hum of modern life, Alessandra zipped through the crowded streets on her battered Vespa. The motorcycle, a vibrant mix of colors, bore a deep scratch on its side, a memento from a previous escapade she preferred not to discuss. She was a whirlwind, her dark curls streaming behind her, eyes scanning the city with a familiar, possessive gaze. Near the Trevi Fountain, Ben stood engrossed in his guidebook, oblivious to the chaos around him. He was a study in contrasts, his tweed jacket and round glasses a relic of another time, his clumsy attempts at Italian a charmingly awkward dance. As Alessandra swerved around a group of tourists, she nearly collided with him, her Vespa screeching to a halt mere inches from his knees. "Watch where you're going, idiota!" she snapped, her eyes flashing. Ben looked up, startled, his cheeks flushing. "Mi dispiace, mi dispiace!" he stammered, his Italian as halting as his steps. "I didn't see you." Alessandra raised an eyebrow, switching to English. "You're British, aren't you? What are you doing in Rome?" Ben pushed his glasses up his nose, a nervous habit. "I'm on sabbatical. Researching ancient Roman architecture." She smirked, looking him up and down. "You look like you need a break from your research. Hop on." Before he could protest, she handed him her helmet. He looked at it, then at her, then back at the helmet, as if it were a foreign object. "I couldn't possibly—" "Come on, Professor," she cut him off, revving the engine. "Live a little." With a deep breath, Ben climbed onto the Vespa, his arms tentatively wrapping around her waist. Alessandra grinned, feeling his hesitation. She took off, weaving through the streets with a reckless abandon that made Ben's heart pound. Their first stop was the Pantheon. Alessandra, with a mischievous glint in her eye, dragged him inside, past the security guard who was engrossed in his phone. She led him to the center of the rotunda, looking up at the oculus. "You know, they say if you stand here at noon on your birthday, you'll be struck by lightning." Ben looked at her, then at the oculus, then back at her. "Is that true?" She laughed, a sound like music. "No, of course not. But it's a good story, isn't it?" Next, they ventured to the Colosseum. Alessandra, with a daring wink, suggested they sneak in. Ben, despite his initial reluctance, found himself following her, his heart pounding with a mix of fear and exhilaration. They climbed over a low wall, Alessandra's laughter echoing in the ancient arena. Ben, despite his clumsiness, found himself keeping up, his eyes wide with wonder and adrenaline. As they sat in the stands, Alessandra pulled out a small, intricately carved figurine from her pocket. She held it up, a small smile playing on her lips. "Look what I found," she said, her voice laced with mischief. Ben's eyes widened, but before he could say anything, she tucked it back into her pocket, her eyes dancing with amusement. Their final stop was a small, hidden trattoria in Trastevere. Alessandra ordered for them, her Italian rapid-fire and confident. Ben, despite his initial discomfort, found himself enjoying the meal, the wine, and the company. Alessandra's eyes sparkled in the candlelight, her laughter infectious. As the night wore on, Ben found himself opening up, sharing stories of his research, his life in England. Alessandra listened, her eyes never leaving his face, her expression inscrutable. When he finished, she smiled, a slow, enigmatic smile. "You're not so bad, Professor," she said, her voice soft. Ben, emboldened by the wine and the night, reached out, tucking a stray curl behind her ear. Alessandra's eyes widened, but she didn't pull away. Instead, she leaned into his touch, her eyes never leaving his. The moment was broken by the sound of a police siren. Alessandra's eyes widened, and she jumped up, pulling Ben with her. "Time to go," she said, her voice breathless. They rushed out of the trattoria, Alessandra's laughter echoing in the narrow streets. Ben, despite his initial reluctance, found himself laughing too, the thrill of the chase coursing through his veins. They ran, their hands entwined, their hearts pounding in sync. As they reached the Trevi Fountain, Alessandra turned to him, her eyes shining. "Well, Professor, that was quite the adventure, wasn't it?" Ben, breathless, looked at her, his heart pounding. "Yes, it was," he said, his voice soft. Alessandra smiled, a slow, enigmatic smile. "Goodnight, Ben," she said, before turning and disappearing into the night. Ben stood there, his heart pounding, his mind racing. He had come to Rome for research, for solitude. But he had found something else entirely. He had found Alessandra, a whirlwind of energy and mischief, a woman who had turned his world upside down in a single day. As he walked back to his hotel, he couldn't help but smile, the thrill of the day still coursing through his veins. He had no idea what the future held, but he knew one thing for sure. He wanted more of Alessandra. More of her laughter, her mischief, her unpredictability. He wanted more of her, period. And as he drifted off to sleep, he couldn't help but wonder what tomorrow would bring. Would Alessandra be there, ready to sweep him off his feet again? Or would she disappear, as suddenly and as mysteriously as she had appeared? Only time would tell. But one thing was for sure. Ben was no longer just a British academic on sabbatical. He was a man in love, a man captivated by a woman who had turned his world upside down. And he wouldn't have it any other way.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is serviceable but shallow. It hits the prompt's beats mechanically: near-collision at the Trevi, Vespa tour, Pantheon, Colosseum, trattoria, parting. However, the scenes are compressed into summary rather than vivid dramatized moments — the prompt asked for "short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges," and the response mostly narrates in past-perfect summary ("Ben, despite his initial reluctance, found himself..."), a phrase repeated nearly verbatim three times. The kleptomania seed is handled with a single figurine moment, which is a decent subtle touch, but it's dropped rather than threaded through the day. The "sneaking into the Colosseum" is implausible and glossed over in two sentences. Alessandra's Italian is minimal; the culture-clash is asserted rather than shown. Dialogue is thin and generic ("Live a little," "You're not so bad, Professor") — functional but never distinctive or witty despite Alessandra being described as sharp-tongued. The ending is the weakest section: heavy telling ("He was a man in love"), rhetorical questions, and a tidy epilogue that wraps up ambiguity the prompt explicitly requested. Ben's transformation from cautious academic to "man in love" is asserted rather than earned through escalating concrete moments. The police siren is a convenient, unearned plot device. Repetitive phrasing ("eyes widened," "heart pounding," "enigmatic smile") and clichés ("a sound like music," "turned his world upside down") abound. Prose is clean and readable, tone consistent, coherent throughout, and the pacing never becomes incoherent — but it reads like a competent first draft, not a story with texture, specificity, or genuine tension. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 48.7
Prompt:
Cozy spacepunk The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I wipe down the counter with a damp cloth, the neon lights of the holographic signs reflecting off the grimy bar top. The usual crowd is here tonight—Grit, the grizzled miner with a knack for trouble; Lyra, the smooth-talking merchant with secrets in her smile; and a few others whose names I can't quite remember. The Outpost is alive with the hum of chatter and the clink of glasses, a comforting sound that's become my lullaby. Suddenly, a glass shatters somewhere in the back. I glance over, but it's just Grit, shrugging off the accident with a mumbled apology. No harm done. Then, a stranger slides onto a barstool, tentacled dreads askew and eyes wild. He looks like he's seen better days, or maybe worse. I raise an eyebrow, waiting. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double," he says, his voice hoarse. I pour the drink, sliding it over to him. "Rough day?" He downs the whisky in one gulp, then nods. "You could say that." I lean in, curious. "Trouble on the rim?" He hesitates, then shakes his head. "Trouble everywhere. But this... this is different. There's a bounty on my head." I raise an eyebrow. "A bounty? For what?" He looks around, lowering his voice. "I stole something. Something valuable. Something that could change the balance of power out here." I whistle low. "Sounds like a mess." He nods, signaling for another drink. I pour it, my mind racing. A bounty hunter's paradise, the Outpost. If word gets out, he's a dead man. "Who's after you?" I ask, keeping my voice casual. He shrugs. "The usual suspects. Mercenaries, bounty hunters, maybe even the Corporate Police. They've got a lot of firepower." I lean back, crossing my arms. "You're in deep, stranger." He nods, taking another swig. "I know. But I can't go back. Not after what I saw." I tilt my head, intrigued. "Saw what?" He looks at me, his eyes distant. "Things. Things that shouldn't exist. Experiments gone wrong. Weapons... things worse than weapons." I shudder, not wanting to imagine what he's talking about. The rim is full of horrors, but some are worse than others. "Look," he says, leaning in. "I need help. I need to lay low, figure out my next move." I shake my head. "I can't get involved in this. I've got enough trouble keeping this place running." He looks around, desperate. "Please. I'll pay. Whatever you want." I sigh, running a hand through my hair. "It's not about the money. It's about staying alive. If they find you here, they'll burn this place to the ground." He slams his fist on the bar. "I can't just walk away! I know too much!" I hold up my hands, trying to calm him down. "I get it. But I can't help you." He looks at me, pleading. "Please. Just let me stay here. I'll keep a low profile. I won't cause any trouble." I hesitate, then sigh. "Fine. But you're on your own. I can't be seen helping you." He nods, relief flooding his face. "Thank you." I pour him another drink, my mind racing. This is trouble. Big trouble. But what choice do I have? The Outpost is my home, and I can't just turn my back on someone in need. Grit walks over, his eyes narrowing as he sees the stranger. "Who's this, Nets?" I shrug, nonchalant. "Just a traveler passing through." Grit grunts, not looking convinced. "Keep your eyes open, Nets. Trouble has a way of finding us out here." I nod, watching as he walks away. Great. Just what I need. More trouble. I turn back to the stranger, who's already looking better. "Stay out of sight. Use the back rooms. And for the love of the stars, keep your tentacles to yourself." He nods, a small smile playing on his lips. "Thank you, Nets." I sigh, pouring myself a drink. This night just got a lot more complicated. Lyra sidles up to the bar, her eyes sparkling with curiosity. "Who's the new meat, Nets?" I roll my eyes. "Just a traveler. Nothing to see here." She raises an eyebrow, not buying it. "Uh-huh. And I'm the queen of the Andromeda galaxy." I sigh, knowing she won't drop it. "Fine. He's in trouble. Big trouble. But I can't get involved." She leans in, her voice low. "But you are involved, aren't you? You always are." I glare at her. "I'm not getting involved. I'm just... letting him stay here. For now." She nods, understanding. "Be careful, Nets. You know how this place is. Trouble has a way of sticking around." I nod, watching as the stranger disappears into the back rooms. This is going to be a long night. The night wears on, the usual drunken antics and bar fights breaking out. I keep an eye on the stranger, making sure he stays out of sight. So far, so good. But as the night winds down and the patrons start to leave, I can't shake the feeling of dread in my stomach. This is just the beginning. I can feel it. As the last of the patrons stumble out, I lock the doors, turning to the stranger. He's sitting in the corner, his tentacles coiled tightly around him. "Alright," I say, walking over. "You can stay here tonight. But tomorrow, you're on your own." He looks up at me, gratitude in his eyes. "Thank you, Nets. You have no idea what this means to me." I sigh, sitting down across from him. "I have some idea. But I can't help you beyond this. You're on your own." He nods, understanding. "I know. And I appreciate it. More than you know." I stand up, walking back to the bar. "Get some rest. Tomorrow's a new day." He nods, settling in for the night. I watch him for a moment, then turn away, my mind racing. This is going to be a long night. And an even longer tomorrow. But for now, all I can do is hope that whatever trouble he's brought with him stays away. At least for tonight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the basic brief: first person, present tense, a stranger arrives with a bounty/secret, conflict established and left unresolved, and dialogue-heavy (likely >60%, actually overshooting). However, execution is flat and generic. The setting never feels like "cozy spacepunk" or even a distinct asteroid-belt outpost — descriptions are minimal (neon lights, grimy bar top, clink of glasses), with no sensory worldbuilding or atmosphere beyond stock phrases. The stranger is nameless and vague; his secrets are withheld through clichés ("Things that shouldn't exist"). Nets' characterization is thin — she claims to have a past and flaws, but the prompt's seed material is barely leveraged; her refusal-then-acceptance of the stranger happens with almost no internal struggle beyond one sigh. The dialogue is the weakest element: repetitive, expository, lacking subtext or character voice. Lines like "Trouble everywhere. But this... this is different" and "I can't get involved in this" read as placeholders. The bartender's repeated flip-flops ("I can't help you" / "Fine") are inconsistent without being meaningfully conflicted. Grit and Lyra are walking archetypes — "the grizzled miner with a knack for trouble," "the smooth-talking merchant with secrets in her smile" — whose only function is to warn Nets that trouble is coming, twice, in nearly identical words. Structurally, the story meanders: the same beat (stranger begs, Nets refuses/half-agrees, side character warns of trouble) repeats three or four times. The ending restates the obvious rather than escalating tension. There are no vivid images, no emotional complexity, no surprises, and the "long night" closer is repeated verbatim. Prose is serviceable but bland, with heavy reliance on filtering ("I feel," "I watch," "I can't shake the feeling"). It is coherent and grammatically competent, which earns it moderate scores on mechanics, but it reads like a serviceable genre exercise rather than an engaging chapter. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 52.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The sun is a brutal bastard today, beating down on the concrete like it's got a personal grudge against me. I squint against the glare, my backpack feeling heavier with each step. The saxophone wails in the background, a mournful tune that matches the storm raging inside me. I'm in New Orleans, of all places. The city of jazz and voodoo and who the hell knows what else. I'm two states away from the shitstorm I left behind, but the echoes of Mom's screams and Dad's silent, judgmental stares are still ringing in my ears. I've been walking for what feels like hours, my stomach growling like a wild animal. I've got a few bucks in my pocket, enough for a meal, maybe two if I'm lucky. But I need to find somewhere to crash tonight. Somewhere safe. The thought makes me snort. Safe. Right. Like there's such a thing in this world. I turn down a side street, away from the tourist traps and into a more rundown area. The buildings are close together, leaning in like they're sharing secrets. The air is thick with humidity and the scent of something sweet and spicy. My mouth waters, but I push the hunger down. I need to find a place to stay first. As I round a corner, I almost collide with a kid about my age. He's got messy dark hair and eyes that are too big for his face. He's holding a skateboard, his fingers tracing the edges nervously. He looks up at me, and for a second, we just stare at each other. Then he smiles, a quick, nervous grin. "Hey," he says. "You new here?" I shrug, not trusting my voice. He nods, like he understands. "Yeah, I thought so. You look like you're lost. I'm Jake, by the way." "Taylor," I mutter, shifting my backpack. "And I'm not lost. Just... exploring." Jake laughs, a sound that's surprisingly warm. "Exploring, huh? Well, welcome to the French Quarter. It's a trip, isn't it?" I don't know what to say to that, so I just nod. Jake seems to take that as an invitation to keep talking. "So, what brings you to New Orleans? Running from something? Or someone?" I bristle at that, my hackles rising. "Why do you assume I'm running?" Jake holds up his hands in surrender. "Hey, no offense. It's just... you've got that look. Like you're on the run. I know it when I see it." I relax slightly, but my guard is still up. "And what look is that?" Jake shrugs. "The lost look. The 'I don't belong here' look. The 'I'm running from something' look." I snort. "Well, aren't you observant." Jake grins. "Yeah, I am. So, what's your story?" I hesitate, then decide to hell with it. What's the worst that can happen? "I'm trans. I came out to my family a couple of days ago. It didn't go well. So, I left." Jake's eyes widen, but he nods. "Yeah, I get it. I'm... I'm gay. My parents found out, and they freaked. Told me I was sick, that I needed help. So, I left." We stand there in silence for a moment, the saxophone's mournful tune filling the air between us. I feel a strange sense of camaraderie, like we're both on the same team, fighting the same battle. "So, where are you staying?" I ask. Jake shrugs. "Here and there. Sometimes I crash with friends, sometimes I find a place to squat. It's not great, but it's better than being at home." I nod, feeling a pang of envy. At least he has friends. I have no one. "Do you know of any places I can stay? Somewhere safe?" Jake thinks for a moment, then nods. "There's this place, a squat downtown. It's not great, but it's better than sleeping on the streets. I can take you there if you want." I hesitate, then nod. "Yeah, okay. Thanks." Jake smiles, and we set off down the street. As we walk, I can't help but feel a sense of unease. I don't know Jake, and I don't know if I can trust him. But I don't have many options, and he seems genuine enough. As we walk, Jake points out landmarks, tells me stories about the city. I listen, half-heartedly, my mind racing. I'm in a strange city, with a stranger, and I have no idea what's going to happen next. But for the first time since I left home, I feel a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, I can make it here. Maybe I can find a place to belong. We turn down a narrow alley, the buildings looming over us like giants. Jake leads me to a door, knocked on it softly. After a moment, it opens, revealing a tall, thin man with a shaved head and a piercing in his eyebrow. "Hey, Jake," he says, his voice gruff. "Who's this?" "This is Taylor," Jake says. "They're new. Need a place to stay." The man looks me up and down, then nods. "Alright. Come on in." I follow Jake inside, my heart pounding. The room is dimly lit, filled with the scent of incense and something sweet and spicy. There are people everywhere, sitting on the floor, leaning against the walls. They all look up as we enter, their eyes curious. Jake leads me to a corner, where there's a pile of blankets and pillows. "Here you go," he says. "It's not much, but it's better than the streets." I nod, feeling a lump form in my throat. "Thanks, Jake. I appreciate it." Jake smiles, then turns to leave. "I'll see you around, Taylor. Welcome to New Orleans." As Jake disappears into the crowd, I sink down onto the blankets, my mind racing. I'm in a strange city, with strange people, and I have no idea what's going to happen next. But for the first time since I left home, I feel a sense of belonging. Maybe, just maybe, I can make it here. Maybe I can find a place to call home. The saxophone's mournful tune fades into the background, replaced by the hum of voices and the scent of incense. I close my eyes, letting the sounds and smells wash over me. I'm safe, for now. And that's enough. But as I drift off to sleep, I can't shake the feeling of unease. I don't know who to trust, and I don't know what dangers lie ahead. But I'm here, and I'm not going back. I'm gone south, and I'm staying that way. No matter what happens, I'm not going back to the life I left behind. I'm Taylor, and I'm trans, and I'm here to stay. And nothing, and no one, is going to change that.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent but fairly generic runaway narrative. It follows the prompt's broad instructions: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, a day in New Orleans, meeting another runaway (Jake) with issues and secrets, internal monologue, and dialogue. However, several prompt elements are underdelivered. Jake's "secrets" are revealed almost instantly and flatly (a mirror-image coming-out story), which flattens the tension the prompt asked for — Taylor "not knowing who to trust" is stated repeatedly rather than dramatized. The squat's inhabitants, including the pierced man, are sketchy non-entities posing mild menace that never materializes. Voice: Taylor's opening voice has some bite ("The sun is a brutal bastard," "shitstorm"), but it softens into bland, safe narration as the chapter progresses. The internal monologue leans heavily on told emotions ("I feel a strange sense of camaraderie," "I feel a glimmer of hope," "I feel a sense of belonging") rather than shown ones. The emotional arc resolves too quickly and too easily — Taylor goes from paranoid to "I feel a sense of belonging" within a single conversation and a pile of blankets, which is an unearned transformation and an incongruent ending positivity given the setup's intensity. Dialogue is serviceable but weak: Jake speaks in exposition-friendly lines ("You've got that look... I know it when I see it"), and the mutual disclosure scene is rushed and unnatural — two strangers trading trauma stories within minutes. The prose is clean and readable, with a few nice touches (buildings "leaning in like they're sharing secrets," the recurring saxophone motif), but also repetitive — "something sweet and spicy" appears twice, and the "Maybe, just maybe, I can make it here" construction is used nearly verbatim twice in a row. The ending's declarative affirmation ("I'm Taylor, and I'm trans, and I'm here to stay") is tidy and sentimental, resolving tension the story hadn't genuinely worked through. Positives: coherent structure, consistent if diluted tone, appropriate length, some atmospheric grounding in New Orleans, and a believable enough premise. Negatives: predictability, tell-don't-show emotion, rushed trust-building, flat secondary characters, and an ending that hands Taylor peace the narrative didn't earn. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 39.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
In the remnants of what was once a bustling city, now known as the Rust, Midas and Chewy sat in their makeshift home, a former fast-food joint called "The Greasy Spoon." The apocalypse had come and gone, leaving behind a world where technology was as rare as a sunny day in a perpetual storm. Midas, a man with a perpetual scowl and a knack for finding trouble, was nursing a cup of lukewarm tea. Chewy, an animatronic stuffed koala from a bygone era, was perched on the counter, his mechanical eyes blinking in a rhythmic pattern that was supposed to mimic thoughtfulness. "Right," Midas said, rubbing his temples. "Today's mission: find this supposed refuge. According to the graffiti, it's hidden in the wilds, beyond the Rust." Chewy tilted his head, a small whirring sound emanating from his neck. "Beep-boop. Adventure awaits, Midas. But remember, the last time we followed a cryptic message, we ended up in a pit of angry badgers." Midas sighed. "Yes, well, we can't stay here forever. We need supplies, and if this refuge exists, it might have what we need." They set off, navigating the treacherous streets of the Rust. The city was a labyrinth of crumbling buildings and twisted metal, a testament to the folly of mankind's reliance on technology. Chewy, with his built-in compass and night vision, led the way, his mechanical paws clicking against the concrete. Their journey took them through the remnants of a once-thriving shopping district, now a graveyard of rusted cars and shattered dreams. They encountered various hazards, from roving bands of scavengers to mutated creatures that lurked in the shadows. But they pressed on, driven by the promise of a refuge. After what felt like hours, they finally reached the edge of the Rust. Beyond lay the wilds, a vast expanse of untamed nature that was as dangerous as it was beautiful. They ventured forth, Chewy's mechanical eyes scanning the horizon for any sign of the refuge. They didn't have to wait long. Soon, they stumbled upon a hidden path, overgrown with weeds and vines. It led them to a clearing, where they found a small, dilapidated cabin. The door was ajar, and a faint light flickered from within. Midas and Chewy exchanged a glance. "Well, here goes nothing," Midas muttered, pushing the door open. Inside, they found a man, huddled over a small fire. He looked up as they entered, his eyes wide with surprise. "Who are you?" he demanded. Midas held up his hands in a placating gesture. "We're just travelers, looking for a refuge. We saw the graffiti and followed it here." The man's expression softened. "Ah, yes. The graffiti. It was a test, you see. To see if you were worthy of finding this place." Chewy tilted his head. "Beep-boop. And are we worthy?" The man chuckled. "Yes, I believe you are. Welcome to the Refuge of the Forgotten. Here, you will find everything you need to survive in this post-apocalyptic world." Midas and Chewy were shown to a room, where they found a stockpile of supplies: food, water, tools, and even a few books. They were overjoyed, their mission a success. But their joy was short-lived. As they explored the refuge, they discovered that it was not as idyllic as it seemed. The man, it turned out, was not a benevolent savior, but a mad scientist, conducting experiments on the refugees in his care. He had lured them there with the promise of safety, only to subject them to his twisted whims. Midas and Chewy, realizing the truth, decided to make a run for it. But the mad scientist was not about to let them go so easily. He set his mutated creations upon them, and a chaotic chase ensued. They fought their way through the refuge, dodging lasers, avoiding traps, and battling mutated creatures. Chewy, with his mechanical agility, was a formidable fighter, his paws transforming into blades that sliced through their enemies with ease. Midas, though not as agile, was no slouch in a fight, his fists and feet a blur of motion. Finally, after what felt like an eternity, they reached the entrance of the refuge. The mad scientist, enraged, appeared before them, a twisted grin on his face. "You can't escape me," he cackled. "I am the master of this place, and you are my prisoners!" Midas, panting, looked at Chewy. "Any ideas?" Chewy tilted his head, his mechanical eyes glowing. "Beep-boop. I have an idea. But it's risky." Midas nodded. "Do it." Chewy's eyes flashed, and suddenly, the refuge was plunged into darkness. The mad scientist, disoriented, stumbled around, his cackles turning into screams of frustration. Midas and Chewy, taking advantage of the chaos, made a run for it, disappearing into the wilds. They returned to the Rust, battered and bruised, but alive. Their mission had been a success, but at a great cost. They had found a refuge, only to discover that it was a trap. But they had also found something else: a renewed sense of purpose. They would continue to explore the wilds, searching for a true refuge, a place where they could live in peace. And so, Midas and Chewy, the unlikely duo, continued their journey, their bond stronger than ever. They had faced the apocalypse and survived, and they would continue to do so, no matter what challenges lay ahead. For they were survivors, and they would not go down without a fight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The story fulfills the basic structural brief — deliberation at home base, a mission that goes sideways, a return home worse for wear — but does so in the most generic way possible. The requested Pratchett-esque wry, dry voice is almost entirely absent; the prose reads like a competent but flavorless summary of an adventure rather than a comic story. There are a few gestures at humor (the angry badgers, "Beep-boop"), but the jokes are sparse and underdeveloped, and Chewy's animatronic nature is used mostly as a plot convenience (compass, night vision, blade-paws, EMP eyes) rather than as comic material. The pacing is severely rushed: the middle section compresses what should be the story's meat — the journey, the discovery of the refuge's true nature, the fight, the escape — into a few flat paragraphs of summary. "They encountered various hazards" and "a chaotic chase ensued" are textbook tell-don't-show. The mad scientist twist is telegraphed and clichéd ("twisted grin," "cackled"), and the refuge plot resolves with no cleverness, just an EMP and a run for it. The ending drifts into unearned uplift: "their bond stronger than ever," "a renewed sense of purpose," "they would not go down without a fight" — a string of hollow inspirational clichés that contradict the wry, worse-for-wear tone the prompt requested. The characters are thin; Midas is defined only by his scowl and "knack for trouble" (stated, never demonstrated), and Chewy has no personality beyond "beep-boop." Dialogue is functional at best and often expository ("It was a test, you see. To see if you were worthy"). Imagery is minimal and stock ("graveyard of rusted cars and shattered dreams," "labyrinth of crumbling buildings"). The prose is competent grammatically but flat, with repeated sentence rhythms ("They fought... They returned... They had found..."). The word count is roughly on target, which is one of the few instructions honored precisely. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 49.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door of *Cyfrol a Chwpan* chimed softly, announcing the arrival of a customer. Elara, the bookstore owner, looked up from her worn copy of *The Mabinogion* to see a tall, disheveled figure slipping inside. She recognized him immediately—Rhys Morgan, the famous actor known for his roguish charm and leading roles in blockbuster films. He was supposed to be filming in Cardiff, not hiding in her small-town bookstore in the heart of Wales. Rhys scanned the room, his eyes landing on Elara. He offered a charming smile, but she merely raised an eyebrow, unperturbed. "Can I help you find something, Mr. Morgan?" she asked, her voice cool and composed. Rhys chuckled, running a hand through his tousled hair. "Just Rhys, please. And I'm not sure. I was hoping to escape the... noise outside. Thought a bookstore might be a good place to hide." Elara nodded, gesturing to the shelves. "Well, you've come to the right place. What do you like to read?" Rhys shrugged, leaning against the counter. "I'm not really sure. I've always been more of a... people person. Books and I haven't exactly seen eye to eye." Elara smirked, pushing her glasses up her nose. "Well, maybe it's time you gave them a chance. What about poetry? It's a good place to start." Rhys raised an eyebrow. "Poetry? Really? Isn't that a bit... dry?" Elara laughed, a genuine sound that made Rhys's heart flutter. "Depends on the poet. Have you ever read Dylan Thomas?" Rhys shook his head. "Can't say I have." Elara stood up, walking over to a shelf. "He's a Welsh poet. Quite famous. His work is... passionate, intense. It might suit you." Rhys followed her, watching as she pulled out a slim volume. "Passionate, huh? I can do passionate." Elara handed him the book, their fingers brushing briefly. Rhys felt a spark, but Elara seemed unaffected. "Here you go. *Death and Entrances*. It's a good place to start." Rhys opened the book, flipping through the pages. "So, what's your story, Elara? How did you end up running a bookstore in the middle of nowhere?" Elara leaned against the shelf, crossing her arms. "It's a long story. Let's just say I needed a change of scenery. This place... it's quiet. Peaceful. I like it." Rhys nodded, sensing there was more to the story. "And what about you? What's your story, Rhys Morgan, the famous actor?" Rhys sighed, running a hand through his hair. "I'm just a guy who got lucky. I mean, I've always loved acting, but I never thought it would take me this far. Sometimes I feel like I'm just playing a role, you know? Like I'm not really... me." Elara looked at him, her expression softening. "Maybe you just need to find the right script. Something that speaks to you, deep down." Rhys met her gaze, feeling a connection he hadn't felt in a long time. "Maybe you're right. Maybe I just need to find the right... story." Elara smiled, turning away. "Well, you're in the right place for that. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have some work to do." Rhys watched her go, feeling a strange mix of frustration and attraction. He opened the book, beginning to read. The words were intense, passionate, just like Elara had said. He found himself getting lost in the poetry, forgetting about the paparazzi outside, forgetting about his fame, his roles, his life. For the first time in a long time, he felt... at peace. Elara, meanwhile, was trying to focus on her work. But her mind kept drifting back to Rhys. She couldn't deny that she found him attractive, charming even. But she also saw the fragility in him, the need for validation. She knew that kind of need, had seen it in herself. It was a dangerous thing, a slippery slope that could lead to heartache. She thought back to her own past, to the man who had broken her heart, who had fed on her need for love and approval. She had sworn never to let that happen again. And yet, here she was, feeling a pull towards Rhys, a man who was the embodiment of everything she had sworn to avoid. She shook her head, pushing the thoughts away. She had a bookstore to run, a life to live. She didn't have time for a famous actor, no matter how charming he was. Rhys, sensing her withdrawal, put the book down. "Elara, wait. I'm sorry if I overstepped. I just... I don't get to meet people like you very often. People who see me, not the actor." Elara turned to him, her expression soft. "Rhys, I see you. But I also see the paparazzi outside, the fame, the fortune. I see the danger in all of that. I can't... I won't get involved in that." Rhys nodded, understanding. "I get it. But can we at least be friends? I could use a friend right now." Elara smiled, her resolve weakening. "Friends. I can do friends." Rhys grinned, holding out his hand. "Friends. It's a start." Elara took his hand, feeling that spark again. But this time, she didn't pull away. Instead, she held on, just a little longer. "It's a start," she agreed. As they stood there, hand in hand, the bell above the door chimed again. This time, it was a customer, a regular who came in every week. She looked at Rhys, then at Elara, her eyes widening in surprise. "Well, isn't this a surprise," she said, a smile spreading across her face. Elara laughed, pulling her hand away from Rhys. "Yes, it is. Rhys, this is Mrs. Davies. She's one of our regulars." Rhys smiled, extending his hand. "Nice to meet you, Mrs. Davies." Mrs. Davies took his hand, her eyes twinkling. "And you, Rhys Morgan. It's not every day we get a famous actor in our little bookstore." Rhys chuckled, looking at Elara. "No, it's not. But I'm glad I did. I think I might have found my new favorite place." Elara smiled, feeling a warmth in her chest. "I'm glad to hear that. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have some work to do." Rhys nodded, picking up the book of poetry. "I'll be here. Reading. Getting to know Dylan Thomas." Elara laughed, walking away. "Good. I think you'll like him." As she disappeared into the back, Rhys looked down at the book, then out the window at the paparazzi. He thought about his life, his fame, his roles. And then he thought about Elara, about the peace he felt in this little bookstore, about the connection he felt with her. He opened the book, beginning to read again. The words were intense, passionate, just like Elara. And for the first time in a long time, Rhys felt like he was exactly where he was meant to be.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is competent but shallow. It meets surface requirements: Wales setting, actor fleeing paparazzi, bookstore owner, dialogue-heavy. However, several core characterization instructions are underdelivered. The actor's "rogue with fragile ego needing everyone to like him" is only faintly present; his charm offensive never really launches, and Elara's immunity never provokes genuine derailing—he simply becomes sincere too quickly and easily. The required "charged undercurrent of unspoken chemistry" is stated rather than dramatized ("feeling a spark," "feeling a connection"). Elara's flustered interior is told in a long exposition block about her past heartbreak, which arrives from nowhere and reads as backstory dump rather than organic development. Her emotional pivot from "I won't get involved" to "friends" happens within a paragraph—unearned transformation. Dialogue is serviceable but generic; characters speak in interchangeable, mildly quippy lines with no distinct voices. Rhys's voice could be anyone's. The Mrs. Davies interruption is a limp ending beat. Prose is plain, with repeated constructions ("running a hand through his hair" twice), repetitive interior summarizing ("for the first time in a long time" twice verbatim). Errors: Rhys is asked "what's your story, Rhys Morgan" by the narration attributing Elara's question to Rhys—a confusing slip. The Mabinogion and Dylan Thomas references are nice Welsh touches, though "Death and Entrances" framing is fine. The ending wraps everything in cozy neatness—peace, connection, belonging—without the scene having done work to earn it. Emotionally flat, tell-heavy, unsurprising, but coherent and readable. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 30.0
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.

[Analysis] The response begins with some atmospheric promise — the descent into the underhold, the torchlit shadows, the scent of ozone — but quickly deteriorates into generic genre filler and, catastrophically, into a degenerating loop of repeated sentences in the second half. Instruction adherence is poor. The prompt specifies Aya is captured and *unmasked*, a pivotal beat that would expose her aristocratic identity and tie directly into her negotiation of her value as a hostage (her family name, ransom potential, connections). The response never unmasks her; Elara simply knows her name, which undercuts the entire premise of Aya moonlighting masked. The negotiation Aya offers is about "information" and "immateria knowledge" rather than her hostage value, and her internal grappling with the consequences of her guild role being exposed — a core emotional requirement — is absent. Katra and Simeon are nameless props with no dialogue whatsoever, despite the prompt's demand for authentic character voices and heavy dialogue. The Victorian/whalepunk aesthetic is reduced to a single foghorn (repeated five times) and some iron doors; no brass, oil, steel, or gothic texture of note. The scythan artifact is mentioned once and dropped. The dialogue that exists is functional but flat: Elara speaks in stock villain clichés ("Well, well, well," "I've been playing this game longer than you've been alive"), and Aya's lines are generic negotiation boilerplate. No character has a distinct voice. Structurally, the piece collapses entirely. From roughly the midpoint onward, the text enters a literal copy-paste loop: "She had to find a way out... She had to find a way to prove her worth... The distant foghorn sounded again..." repeated verbatim perhaps a dozen times. This is a severe generation failure, destroying coherence, pacing, and any reader engagement. The ending is not an ending at all. [Analysis] The piece opens with a serviceable scene-setting at "The Rusty Nail" and initially follows the prompt's premise: both characters hired for the same bounty, meeting in a seedy bar, drinking, mutual wariness. However, the story quickly derails. The motel room scene — which the prompt specifies as the culmination of gunplay and unresolved sexual tension — instead features a rushed, out-of-character bounty kill (Revy executing a surrendered man contradicts her established pragmatism; bounty hunters don't kill bounties, which both characters would know), and then the story inexplicably returns to the bar for the "standoff," abandoning the motel entirely. The most glaring flaw is the dialogue. From roughly the midpoint onward, the piece collapses into a repetitive loop of nearly identical exchanges: "And what if I am?" / "Then you'll have to prove it" / "eyes narrowed" / "lips curled into a smirk" / "eyes flashed with surprise and anger." Entire paragraphs are duplicated verbatim. This reads like a model losing coherence and padding to word count. The final third is essentially the same conversation repeated four or five times with no progression. Characterization is surface-level. Spike's fatalism is reduced to quoting his catchphrase once. Revy's complexity (her vulnerability, her Rock-related softness) is gestured at with a single "flicker of vulnerability" that is immediately dropped. Neither character behaves believably: Revy killing a bounty they were both hired to capture destroys the premise, and Spike's response is oddly mild. The "attraction" is stated rather than dramatized — "he felt a strange attraction to her" is pure tell. The prose is functional at best, with clichés ("the tension was electric," "the air was thick with smoke") and no distinctive voice. Present tense is mostly maintained, though slips toward mechanical narration. The ending — Revy simply walking away after the loop finally breaks — is abrupt and unearned, resolving nothing in a way that feels like giving up rather than deliberate ambiguity. The first third is competent genre filler; everything after the motel is a repetitive, incoherent descent. This is a weak piece with severe structural failure. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 50.7
Prompt:
Fok Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The night was a thick blanket, smothering the world in silence and darkness. I remember the cold, how it bit into my cheeks and made my breath visible in the air. It was the mid-1990s, and I was in rural northern Sweden, a world away from the neon lights and bustle of Stockholm. My parents had uprooted us for my father's job, and I was left to navigate the stark, unfamiliar landscape of this small village. Astrid, my new friend, had a way of making the mundane seem magical. She was tall and lanky, with wild hair that seemed to defy gravity. Her eyes held a spark that was both inviting and unsettling. She claimed her grandmother had taught her ancient practices, rituals passed down through generations. I was skeptical, but there was something thrilling about the danger, the forbidden allure of it all. That night, Astrid had convinced me to participate in Útiseta, an ancient ritual involving sitting out on a burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." I remember the way she said it, her voice a mix of teenage rebellion and eerie tradition. We had spent the evening preparing, gathering items from Astrid's grandmother's house—a small bundle of dried herbs, a candle, and a worn, leather-bound book filled with symbols and incantations. The burial mound was a short walk from Astrid's house, a silent sentinel in the moonlight. It was an ancient thing, covered in moss and lichen, its shape barely discernible in the darkness. Astrid led the way, her steps sure and confident. I followed, my heart pounding in my chest. As we reached the mound, Astrid began to set up. She placed the candle in the center, lighting it with a match. The flame flickered, casting eerie shadows on the ancient stones. She then arranged the herbs in a circle around the candle, their scent filling the air. I watched, a mix of fascination and unease churning in my stomach. Astrid opened the book, her fingers tracing the yellowed pages. She began to chant, her voice low and rhythmic. The words were foreign to me, but there was a power in them, a resonance that seemed to echo from the very earth beneath us. I felt a shiver run down my spine, and I wasn't sure if it was from the cold or something else. I sat down, my back against the cold stone of the mound. Astrid continued her chant, her eyes closed, her body swaying gently. I tried to focus, to let the words wash over me, but my mind was a whirlwind of doubts and fears. Was this all just a game? Or was there something more, something ancient and dangerous? The wind picked up, howling through the trees. The candle flame flickered, casting wild shadows on the stones. I felt a chill, a cold that seemed to seep into my very bones. And then, I heard it—a whisper, faint and distant, like the rustling of leaves. But there were no leaves, only the bare branches of winter. I looked at Astrid, her face illuminated by the candlelight. Her eyes were still closed, her lips moving in silent chant. I wanted to ask her if she heard it too, but the words stuck in my throat. The whisper grew louder, more insistent. It was a voice, I realized, a voice that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. "Who are you?" I whispered, my voice barely audible over the wind. The voice didn't answer, but the whispering grew louder, more insistent. I felt a presence, a cold, heavy weight that seemed to press down on me. I wanted to run, to flee into the safety of the night, but my body was frozen, rooted to the spot. Astrid's eyes snapped open, her gaze locking onto mine. "What's wrong?" she asked, her voice sharp. I couldn't speak, couldn't find the words to describe the terror that gripped me. Astrid looked around, her eyes widening as she took in the scene. The candle flame was dancing wildly, casting eerie shadows on the stones. The wind howled, a mournful, chilling sound. Astrid stood up, her voice rising above the wind. "We're done," she said, her voice firm. "We're leaving." She reached down, grabbing my hand and pulling me to my feet. I stumbled, my legs shaking, my heart pounding. We gathered our things, the book, the herbs, the candle, and fled into the night. As we ran, the whispering faded, the cold lifted, and the wind died down. We didn't speak, our breaths coming in ragged gasps. We reached Astrid's house, the lights warm and inviting. We stumbled inside, our hearts still pounding. Astrid's grandmother was in the kitchen, her eyes wide with concern. "What happened?" she asked, her voice soft. Astrid looked at me, her eyes filled with a mix of fear and excitement. "We did Útiseta," she said, her voice barely a whisper. Her grandmother's face paled, her eyes widening in shock. "You did what?" she asked, her voice sharp. Astrid looked down, her voice soft. "We sat on the mound, we chanted, we tried to... to receive knowledge." Her grandmother's face was a mask of horror. "You foolish children," she said, her voice shaking. "You have no idea what you've done." I remember the way she looked at us, her eyes filled with a mix of fear and anger. She told us stories then, stories of ancient rituals gone wrong, of spirits that had been disturbed, of the dangers of meddling with things we didn't understand. I remember the way her voice shook, the way her hands trembled. And I remember the way I felt, a cold, gnawing fear in the pit of my stomach. As I sit here now, years later, I still wonder about that night. Was it all just a trick of the mind, a product of our overactive imaginations? Or was there something more, something ancient and dangerous that we had stirred? I don't know, and I'm not sure I want to. But I do know this—we had crossed a line that night, a dangerous line that we should never have crossed. And we had paid the price for our foolishness.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece hits the basic plot beats of the prompt: rural northern Sweden, 1990s, Linnea and Astrid, Útiseta on a burial mound, ambiguity between supernatural and psychological. However, the execution is generic and flat. The prose relies heavily on clichés ("heart pounding," "shiver down my spine," "eyes widening," "a world away from the neon lights"). The setting is asserted rather than evoked—there's no specific sensory detail of northern Sweden (no snow texture, no pines, no village texture, no period markers beyond a stated year). The "mid-1990s" is literally stated in the first paragraph rather than shown. The ritual preparations are thin: herbs, a candle, a book. Astrid's "matter-of-fact instructions mixing teenage rebellion with traditional elements" is mostly absent—she's a sketch, and her chant is described but never given content. The mounting tension is rushed; the whispering voice appears quickly and resolves abruptly when Astrid says "We're done." The grandmother scene at the end is a significant deviation from the prompt's focus on the single midnight excursion, and it deflates the ambiguity by having an adult confirm real danger ("You have no idea what you've done")—undermining the requested ambiguity between supernatural and psychological. The ending explicitly tells us "we had paid the price for our foolishness" without showing any price, an unearned dark conclusion. Dialogue is functional but stilted ("You did what?"). Telling dominates showing: emotions are named repeatedly ("fear," "terror gripped me," "unease churning in my stomach"). The retrospective framing is present but transparent to a fault—the present-day reflections are generic. Word count is roughly on target. The piece is coherent and readable but reads like a competent template story with no distinctive voice, no specificity, and a rushed, clichéd climax. I nod, trying to ignore the flutter in my stomach. He moves to the head of the table, his hands gentle yet firm as he adjusts my position.
